title: Karma Yoga
hook: a warm speech at a party, and twenty minutes later, the same man in the parking lot

segments.voice: Yesterday, Karma Yoga and the fly in the honey: drink, but keep your feet on the rim. Did you let one result go before anyone told you how it landed? Day nine hundred forty-four.
screen: `KARMA YOGA.` · `KEEP YOUR FEET ON THE RIM.`

segments.voice: Two scenes from one afternoon. In the first, a man gives the toast at a retirement party. He's funny, he's generous, he names everyone who helped. People wipe their eyes. In the second, twenty minutes later, he's in the parking lot, leaning on his horn at an old man who is backing out too slowly. Which scene is the real him? Early in his talks on Karma Yoga, Vivekananda asks where a person's real character shows, and his answer points away from the toast. Today, where character actually lives.
screen: `A WARM TOAST AT A PARTY.` → `THE SAME MAN IN THE PARKING LOT.` → `WHICH ONE IS HIM?`

segments.voice: The first chapter of Karma Yoga is about what work does to character. And early on, Vivekananda says something that sounds simple and isn't. Don't judge a person by their great moments. Big occasions, he says, can lift almost anyone up for a while; even an ordinary person can be a hero once. Watch them instead doing the most common things. That's where the real character shows. Then he explains why. Every action we take, and every thought we think, leaves a mark on the mind, like a wave on a lake that sinks back down but leaves the water changed. Hindu thought calls these marks samskaras, impressions. And what we call a person's character, he says, is really the sum of these impressions, piled up over time. Good impressions, repeated, make a tendency toward good. Careless ones, repeated, make a tendency too. So the parking lot isn't a slip from the real man. It's a window into the pile. And here's the turn that makes this a yoga and not just a warning. If small actions build character, then small actions are where the work gets done. Not the toast, which happens once. The horn, the email tone, the way you hand someone their change, which happen every day. Karma Yoga, in this chapter, is less about the grand gesture than about the ordinary ones nobody films. Each one is laying down the next layer of who you'll be tomorrow.
screen: `DON'T JUDGE BY THE GREAT MOMENTS.` · `WATCH THE MOST COMMON THINGS.` · `EVERY ACT LEAVES AN IMPRESSION.` · `CHARACTER IS THE PILE OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow down on its own. Bring back one ordinary moment from yesterday: a meal, a commute, a phone call, a line at a counter. Don't pick a big moment. Pick a small one. Replay it slowly. How did you speak? What did your hands do? Was there a flash of impatience, or a small kindness? No need to judge it. Just notice what impression that moment may have left. Then choose one ordinary moment coming up today, and picture doing it with care. If you pray, you can offer that small moment in a prayer you already know. The bell holds the time.
Karma Yoga. The yoga of work, and of the common actions where Vivekananda says character is really built.
Your line: Karma Yoga. Today, pick one ordinary thing you do on autopilot, holding a door, answering a text, and do it as if it counts, because in this chapter, it does. Day nine hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Hindus who read Vivekananda's Karma Yoga in Vedanta study circles discuss its first chapter on character, and some describe the practice as bringing care to everyday work, not only to special occasions.

fork.setup: you want to know what someone is really like. Vivekananda's chapter gives you two places to look. which does he choose?
options: how they do the most ordinary things.
what their friends say at a party.
fork.reveal: he says great occasions can lift almost anyone, even an ordinary person can be a hero once. common actions show the real character.

original.note: Sanskrit: an impression left on the mind by what we do and think.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma yoga is about doing big good deeds.
what it means: every ordinary act leaves an impression, and character is built from them.
what a scholar hears: Vivekananda's first chapter, 'karma in its effect on character', ties work to samskaras, the impressions that make up a person's tendencies.

sources.ref: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 1, Karma in Its Effect on Character
sources.work: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda, vol. 1 (paraphrased)

notes: All paraphrase of Vivekananda's English. Confirm in Karma-Yoga ch. 1: judge a man not by his great performances but by his most common actions; great occasions can rouse even the lowest to greatness; every work and thought leaves an impression (the wave image); character as the sum total of these impressions; good impressions repeated create a tendency to good.

Confirm Vivekananda uses the word samskara in this chapter; if not, the line 'Hindu thought calls these marks samskaras' still stands as a general description but the trapdoor's third floor should be softened.
Original: संस्कार (saṃskāra); confirm spelling and pronunciation guide.
Year-one days 260–266 and 309–314 and year-three days 942–943 used other Karma-Yoga passages; this day avoids them.
Editor pass: the hook no longer claims he opens the talks 'with almost this exact question'; howItsDone drops 'often'.

Audit pass: the wave image said a wave leaves a trace 'on the shore'; Vivekananda's picture is of waves in the mind-lake that subside but leave an impression, so the line now says that. Confirm the wording against Karma-Yoga ch. 1.
